title: Osler nodes, Janeway lesions & splinter haemorrhages
summary: The fingertip and palm signs of infective endocarditis, what they mean, why none of them is diagnostic alone, and why fever plus any of them needs same-day admission.

glance.think: Tender pulp nodules (Osler), painless palm or sole macules (Janeway) or splinters, especially with fever or a murmur.
glance.engine: Immune-complex vasculitis (Osler) and septic micro-emboli (Janeway) from infected heart valves.
glance.backbone: Fever + signs = same-day admission for blood cultures before antibiotics and echocardiography (modified Duke criteria).
glance.never_miss: Endocarditis in injecting drug users, people with prosthetic valves or devices; starting antibiotics before cultures.

what: Classic peripheral signs of **infective endocarditis (IE)**. They are now uncommon (each is seen in <10–15% of modern IE cases) because IE is diagnosed earlier.

list: **Osler nodes:** **tender**, pea-sized red-purple nodules on the **pads of fingers and toes** (and thenar/hypothenar eminences), lasting hours to days.
**Janeway lesions:** **painless**, flat or slightly raised haemorrhagic macules on the **palms and soles**.
**Splinter haemorrhages:** thin, longitudinal, red-brown/black lines in the nail bed, running in the direction of nail growth.
**Osler nodes:** traditionally **immunological** (immune-complex vasculitis); histology also shows microemboli. They count as an **immunological phenomenon** in the Duke criteria.
**Janeway lesions:** **septic microemboli** with dermal microabscesses (a **vascular phenomenon**), so organisms may be cultured from them.
**Splinters:** rupture of longitudinally oriented nail-bed capillaries (trauma) or microemboli/vasculitis.

features: The Osler/Janeway distinction is tender vs painless. Look also for **Roth spots** (retinal haemorrhages with pale centres — fundoscopy), conjunctival petechiae, clubbing (subacute), new murmur, fever, splenomegaly, haematuria, and embolic events (stroke, limb ischaemia).

list: **Endocarditis:** **2023 Duke–ISCVID / ESC 2023 criteria**: **Major:** typical organisms in ≥2 blood cultures; imaging evidence (echo/PET-CT vegetation, abscess, new valvular regurgitation); **Minor:** predisposition (prosthetic valve, previous IE, IV drug use, congenital heart disease, cardiac devices), **fever ≥38 °C**, **vascular phenomena** (major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial haemorrhage, conjunctival haemorrhages, **Janeway lesions**), **immunological phenomena** (glomerulonephritis, **Osler nodes**, Roth spots, positive rheumatoid factor), microbiological evidence not meeting the major criterion
**Tests (hospital):** ≥3 sets of blood cultures **before antibiotics**, echocardiography (TTE → TOE), FBC, CRP, urinalysis.

differentials: **No.** None of the three is specific to IE.

Other causes
rows: SLE, **gonococcaemia**, typhoid, haemolytic anaemia, marantic (non-bacterial thrombotic) endocarditis, infected radial-artery lines (distal emboli), vasculitis
SLE, gonococcaemia, typhoid, other septicaemia, haemolytic anaemia

**Trauma (commonest — manual workers, distal splinters)**, **psoriasis**, **onychomycosis**, eczema, haemodialysis, vasculitis/connective tissue disease, **antiphospholipid syndrome**, trichinosis, high altitude, mitral stenosis, scurvy, drugs (tetracyclines, VEGF-inhibitors such as sunitinib/sorafenib), and some normal elderly people

differentials: **How many splinters matter?** There is **no validated number**. Splinters are more suspicious when they are **new**, **multiple** (several in one nail or across **several nails** — some texts suggest ≥4), **proximal** (rather than distal — trauma), **painful**, and **accompanied by fever, a murmur or IE risk factors**. Context, not count, makes the diagnosis.

list: **Suspected IE** (fever + new murmur or IE risk + embolic/vascular signs) → **same-day hospital assessment**. **Do not start oral antibiotics** before blood cultures — this sterilises cultures and delays diagnosis (a common primary-care pitfall).

**IE prophylaxis (NICE CG64, updated 2016):** antibiotic prophylaxis for dental/other procedures is **not routinely recommended**. Advise high-risk patients on good **dental hygiene**, to avoid body piercing/tattooing, and on **symptoms to report** (persistent fever, night sweats, weight loss).
**People who inject drugs:** harm reduction (needle-exchange, PWID services), awareness of IE (often right-sided, *S. aureus*).

management: Any febrile patient with new splinters/Osler/Janeway lesions, a murmur, a prosthetic valve, IV drug use or embolic events → same day. Isolated distal splinters in a well manual worker → reassure and review.
Recognition and urgent referral; no antibiotic initiation for suspected IE in primary care; counselling of at-risk patients.
red_flags: Fever with a new murmur, splinters or Osler/Janeway lesions: **same-day admission**; do not give antibiotics before blood cultures unless septic.
